A distinct dichotomy emerges in creativity: while LLMs excel in language-based creative tasks, such as storytelling, they struggle with divergent thinking tasks that require real-world context. Nonetheless, studies suggest that LLMs hold considerable potential as collaborators, augmenting creativity in human-machine problem-solving settings. Discussing key limitations, we also offer guidance for future research in areas such as memory, attention, and open-source model development.

papers.title: The Irrationality of Neural Rationale Models
papers.research_question: Does the bottleneck structure of neural rationale models guarantee interpretability, or can they be as non-interpretable as black-box models?
papers.core_contribution: Challenges the assumption that neural rationale models are inherently interpretable by showing that their selectors can be non-interpretable, and demonstrates this through philosophical arguments and empirical instability under perturbations.
papers.conclusion: Neural rationale models are not inherently interpretable by design, and more rigorous analysis is needed to ensure interpretability claims.
papers.key_findings:
Neural rationale models can be as non-interpretable as black-box models if the selector is not understood, as shown by a counter-example where the selector encodes predictions.
Rationale selection is unstable under minimal, meaning-preserving sentence perturbations, with changes often occurring far from the perturbation location.
A user study shows that even with examples, people cannot understand the selector's behavior, performing at random guess level.
The continuous relaxation (CR) model, while more accurate, is less stable in rationale selection compared to the policy gradient (PG) model.
Rationale changes are distributed across sentences and parts of speech, indicating complex selector behavior.
future_direction: More rigorous analysis and evaluation of interpretability in neural rationale models.
papers.abstract: Neural rationale models are popular for interpretable predictions of NLP tasks. In these, a selector extracts segments of the input text, called rationales, and passes these segments to a classifier for prediction. Since the rationale is the only information accessible to the classifier, it is plausibly defined as the explanation. Is such a characterization unconditionally correct? In this paper, we argue to the contrary, with both philosophical perspectives and empirical evidence suggesting that rationale models are, perhaps, less rational and interpretable than expected. We call for more rigorous evaluations of these models to ensure desired properties of interpretability are indeed achieved. The code for our experiments is at https://github.com/yimingz89/N eural-Rationale-Analysis.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Large Language Models Report Subjective Experience Under Self-Referential Processing
papers.research_question: Does sustained self-referential processing systematically increase the likelihood that LLMs claim to have subjective experience, and if so, what are the core statistical and mechanistic dynamics underlying these claims?
papers.core_contribution: Self-referential processing reliably elicits structured first-person reports of subjective experience across LLM families, and these reports are mechanistically gated by deception-related SAE features, show semantic convergence, and generalize to downstream introspection tasks.
papers.conclusion: Self-referential processing is a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable, warranting further scientific and ethical investigation.
papers.key_findings:
Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families.
These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims.
Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition.
The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded.
papers.limitation:
The possibility that the reports are sophisticated roleplay rather than genuine introspection.
Reliance on SAE features from one model (Llama 70B) and the need for cross-architectural validation.
The prompts may trigger finetuned behaviors (e.g., Claude 4 Opus's high baseline claims).
Self-referential prompting does not instantiate architectural recursion but is a behavioral intervention, so it may not correspond to genuine internal integration.
future_direction: Determining whether behavioral attractors correspond to genuine internal integration or merely symbolic simulation.
Cross-architectural validation of SAE feature effects.
Studying self-referential processing at algorithmic and implementation levels.
papers.abstract: Large language models sometimes produce structured, first-person descriptions that explicitly reference awareness or subjective experience. To better understand this behavior, we investigate one theoretically motivated condition under which such reports arise: self-referential processing, a computational motif emphasized across major theories of consciousness. Through a series of controlled experiments on GPT, Claude, and Gemini model families, we test whether this regime reliably shifts models toward first-person reports of subjective experience, and how such claims behave under mechanistic and behavioral probes. Four main results emerge: (1) Inducing sustained self-reference through simple prompting consistently elicits structured subjective experience reports across model families. (2) These reports are mechanistically gated by interpretable sparse-autoencoder features associated with deception and roleplay: surprisingly, suppressing deception features sharply increases the frequency of experience claims, while amplifying them minimizes such claims. (3) Structured descriptions of the self-referential state converge statistically across model families in ways not observed in any control condition. (4) The induced state yields significantly richer introspection in downstream reasoning tasks where self-reflection is only indirectly afforded. While these findings do not constitute direct evidence of consciousness, they implicate self-referential processing as a minimal and reproducible condition under which large language models generate structured first-person reports that are mechanistically gated, semantically convergent, and behaviorally generalizable. The systematic emergence of this pattern across architectures makes it a first-order scientific and ethical priority for further investigation.

papers.title: Compositional Processing Emerges in Neural Networks Solving Math Problems
papers.research_question: Do deep neural networks evaluate arithmetic expressions using the principle of compositionality by encoding and combining partial results?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on math problems can encode partial results of sub-expressions in their internal representations, demonstrating emergent compositional processing.
papers.conclusion: Neural networks can exhibit compositional processing when trained on math problems, though imperfectly, suggesting a blend of compositional and holistic strategies.
papers.key_findings:
Models encode digit quantities in their representations, with vectors organized by numerical value.
Operators encode intermediate arithmetic results, with vector distances correlating with value differences.
These encodings are found in attention vectors, indicating compositional processing.
Compositionality is imperfect, as shown by non-zero correlations across sequences.
Both standard and TP-Transformers exhibit similar patterns of compositional encoding.
papers.limitation:
The observed compositionality is imperfect, with non-zero correlations indicating incomplete separation of sub-expressions.
Models show poor generalization on extrapolation problems with different surface features.
future_direction: Clarify whether scaling leads to human-level compositionality or if explicit design is needed.
papers.abstract: A longstanding question in cognitive science concerns the learning mechanisms underlying compositionality in human cognition. Humans can infer the structured relationships (e.g., grammatical rules) implicit in their sensory observations (e.g., auditory speech), and use this knowledge to guide the composition of simpler meanings into complex wholes. Recent progress in artificial neural networks has shown that when large models are trained on enough linguistic data, grammatical structure emerges in their representations. We extend this work to the domain of mathematical reasoning, where it is possible to formulate precise hypotheses about how meanings (e.g., the quantities corresponding to numerals) should be composed according to structured rules (e.g., order of operations). Our work shows that neural networks are not only able to infer something about the structured relationships implicit in their training data, but can also deploy this knowledge to guide the composition of individual meanings into composite wholes.

papers.title: Do You Trust Me? Cognitive-Affective Signatures of Trustworthiness in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do instruction-tuned LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in narratives, where do these representations emerge across transformer depth, how well can they be decoded, and how do they relate to psychological constructs like fairness and certainty?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs encode perceived trustworthiness in systematic, layer- and head-specific patterns that are linearly decodable and align with psychological constructs like fairness and certainty, demonstrating that trust signals emerge during pretraining without explicit supervision.
papers.conclusion: The findings show that LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals, offering a representational foundation for designing credible and trustworthy AI systems in web applications.
papers.key_findings:
Activation differences between high- and low-trust narratives are observed across models, indicating trust-sensitive features emerge during pretraining.
Trustworthiness is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, with probe performance varying by layer and head.
Fine-tuning with LoRA sharpens existing trust representations rather than restructuring them.
Trust representations are most strongly associated with psychological appraisals like fairness, certainty, and accountability-self.
Nonlinear probes provide only marginal gains, indicating trust information is largely in linearly accessible subspaces.
papers.abstract: Perceived trustworthiness underpins how users navigate online information, yet it remains unclear whether large language models (LLMs),increasingly embedded in search, recommendation, and conversational systems, represent this construct in psychologically coherent ways. We analyze how instruction-tuned LLMs (Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen 2.5 7B, Mistral 7B) encode perceived trustworthiness in web-like narratives using the PEACE-Reviews dataset annotated for cognitive appraisals, emotions, and behavioral intentions. Across models, systematic layer- and head-level activation differences distinguish high- from low-trust texts, revealing that trust cues are implicitly encoded during pretraining. Probing analyses show linearly de-codable trust signals and fine-tuning effects that refine rather than restructure these representations. Strongest associations emerge with appraisals of fairness, certainty, and accountability-self -- dimensions central to human trust formation online. These findings demonstrate that modern LLMs internalize psychologically grounded trust signals without explicit supervision, offering a representational foundation for designing credible, transparent, and trust-worthy AI systems in the web ecosystem. Code and appendix are available at: https://github.com/GerardYeo/TrustworthinessLLM.

papers.title: Linear Representations of Political Perspective Emerge in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Does the activation space of LLMs contain linear representations of political perspective, and can these be used to monitor and steer model outputs?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs possess linear representations of political ideology in their activation space, which can be identified through probing and used to monitor and steer model outputs.
papers.conclusion: LLMs learn linear representations of political perspective, enabling monitoring and steering of ideological slant in generated text.
papers.key_findings:
Linear probes on attention heads can predict U.S. lawmakers' political ideology (DW-NOMINATE scores) with high Spearman correlation (up to ~0.87).
The representations are linear, as non-linear probes do not substantially improve predictive performance.
Probes trained on lawmakers' ideology generalize to predict the political slant of news outlets (Ad Fontes scores).
The learned linear directions can be used to monitor the political slant of generated text token-by-token.
Applying linear interventions to the identified attention heads can steer model outputs toward more liberal or conservative perspectives.
papers.limitation:
The generality of political slant representations varies significantly across nations, with weaker performance for non-U.S. contexts.
Extreme intervention values (alpha < -30 or > 30) often lead to incoherent model outputs.
future_direction: Creation of comprehensive datasets capturing diverse political contexts to improve cross-cultural applicability.
More systematic evaluation of the token-by-token monitoring method.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated the ability to generate text that realistically reflects a range of different subjective human perspectives. This paper studies how LLMs are seemingly able to reflect more liberal versus more conservative viewpoints among other political perspectives in American politics. We show that LLMs possess linear representations of political perspectives within activation space, wherein more similar perspectives are represented closer together. To do so, we probe the attention heads across the layers of three open transformer-based LLMs (Llama-2-7b-chat, Mistral-7b-instruct, Vicuna-7b). We first prompt models to generate text from the perspectives of different U.S. lawmakers. We then identify sets of attention heads whose activations linearly predict those lawmakers' DW-NOMINATE scores, a widely-used and validated measure of political ideology. We find that highly predictive heads are primarily located in the middle layers, often speculated to encode high-level concepts and tasks. Using probes only trained to predict lawmakers' ideology, we then show that the same probes can predict measures of news outlets' slant from the activations of models prompted to simulate text from those news outlets. These linear probes allow us to visualize, interpret, and monitor ideological stances implicitly adopted by an LLM as it generates open-ended responses. Finally, we demonstrate that by applying linear interventions to these attention heads, we can steer the model outputs toward a more liberal or conservative stance. Overall, our research suggests that LLMs possess a high-level linear representation of American political ideology and that by leveraging recent advances in mechanistic interpretability, we can identify, monitor, and steer the subjective perspective underlying generated text.

papers.title: Probing the Geometry of Truth: Consistency and Generalization of Truth Directions in LLMs Across Logical Transformations and Question Answering Tasks
papers.research_question: Do LLMs universally represent truthfulness as a linear feature (truth direction)? Are simple probing techniques sufficiently expressive to identify truth directions? How does the truth direction generalize across logical transformations and question answering tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Consistent truth directions only emerge in capable LLMs and can be identified with simple linear probes; these probes generalize effectively to logical transformations, question answering, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources.
papers.conclusion: Truth directions are present in capable LLMs, can be identified with simple probes, and generalize well, highlighting their potential for eliciting latent knowledge and improving trust in LLM outputs.
papers.key_findings:
Not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions; this property is correlated with model capability, with stronger representations in more capable models.
Simple probes (linear SVM, logistic regression, MLP, mass-mean) are sufficient to identify truth directions when they exist.
Truthfulness probes generalize across logical negation, conjunction, and disjunction.
Truthfulness probes trained on atomic statements generalize to question answering tasks (MMLU, TriviaQA) and contextual knowledge tasks (SciQ, BoolQ, XSum).
Truthfulness probes can be used for selective question answering to filter out false answers, improving answer quality.
papers.limitation:
The term 'truth' may not be exactly what the probes measure; they likely capture an overlap between widely accepted human beliefs and objective truths.
Generalization is only tested on short-form QA; long-form QA and instruction-following tasks are not studied.
The causality of truthfulness probes is unclear; they may capture spuriously-correlated features rather than the target feature.
Computational resources limited evaluation to models up to Llama-3.1-70B, leaving more advanced models like GPT-4 untested.
future_direction: Extend analysis to more complex scenarios such as long-form QA and instruction-following tasks.
Study the causal implications of truth directions to guide LLMs toward more truthful responses.
Test the hypothesis on more advanced models like GPT-4.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are trained on extensive datasets that encapsulate substantial world knowledge. However, their outputs often include confidently stated inaccuracies. Earlier works suggest that LLMs encode truthfulness as a distinct linear feature, termed the "truth direction", which can classify truthfulness reliably. We address several open questions about the truth direction: (i) whether LLMs universally exhibit consistent truth directions; (ii) whether sophisticated probing techniques are necessary to identify truth directions; and (iii) how the truth direction generalizes across diverse contexts. Our findings reveal that not all LLMs exhibit consistent truth directions, with stronger representations observed in more capable models, particularly in the context of logical negation. Additionally, we demonstrate that truthfulness probes trained on declarative atomic statements can generalize effectively to logical transformations, question-answering tasks, in-context learning, and external knowledge sources. Finally, we explore the practical application of truthfulness probes in selective question-answering, illustrating their potential to improve user trust in LLM outputs. These results advance our understanding of truth directions and provide new insights into the internal representations of LLM beliefs. Our code is public at https://github.com/colored-dye/truthfulness_probe_generalization

papers.title: Decoding Emotion in the Deep: A Systematic Study of How LLMs Represent, Retain, and Express Emotion
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly expected to navigate the nuances of human emotion. While research confirms that LLMs can simulate emotional intelligence, their internal emotional mechanisms remain largely unexplored. This paper investigates the latent emotional representations within modern LLMs by asking: how, where, and for how long is emotion encoded in their neural architecture? To address this, we introduce a novel, large-scale Reddit corpus of approximately 400,000 utterances, balanced across seven basic emotions through a multi-stage process of classification, rewriting, and synthetic generation. Using this dataset, we employ lightweight "probes" to read out information from the hidden layers of various Qwen3 and LLaMA models without altering their parameters. Our findings reveal that LLMs develop a surprisingly well-defined internal geometry of emotion, which sharpens with model scale and significantly outperforms zero-shot prompting. We demonstrate that this emotional signal is not a final-layer phenomenon but emerges early and peaks mid-network. Furthermore, the internal states are both malleable (they can be influenced by simple system prompts) and persistent, as the initial emotional tone remains detectable for hundreds of subsequent tokens. We contribute our dataset, an open-source probing toolkit, and a detailed map of the emotional landscape within LLMs, offering crucial insights for developing more transparent and aligned AI systems. The code and dataset are open-sourced.

papers.title: Identifying Cooperative Personalities in Multi-agent Contexts through Personality Steering with Representation Engineering
papers.research_question: How do personality traits, steered via representation engineering, affect LLM behavior and cooperation in multi-agent games like the Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma?
papers.core_contribution: Personality steering using representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, but with a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability to exploitation.
papers.conclusion: Personality steering through representation engineering effectively promotes cooperation in LLM-based multi-agent systems, providing a foundation for future work in cooperative AI agents.
papers.key_findings:
Steering towards agreeableness, conscientiousness, and openness reduces troublemaking rates to zero.
High agreeableness increases exploitability, highlighting a trade-off between cooperation and vulnerability.
Agreeableness and conscientiousness lower lying rates, promoting honesty regardless of opponent behavior.
Models steered towards agreeableness and conscientiousness achieve better collective outcomes but worse individual outcomes.
Personality-steered behavior aligns with human psychological traits in similar contexts.
papers.limitation:
Limited to Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma variants and a single payoff matrix.
Effectiveness across different LLM architectures and tasks remains an open question.
Real-world multi-agent interactions involve more complex incentives.
future_direction: Explore diverse game-theoretic frameworks beyond IPD
Validate results across broader contexts and applications
Investigate effectiveness across different LLM architectures
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) gain autonomous capabilities, their coordination in multi-agent settings becomes increasingly important. However, they often struggle with cooperation, leading to suboptimal outcomes. Inspired by Axelrod's Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma (IPD) tournaments, we explore how personality traits influence LLM cooperation. Using representation engineering, we steer Big Five traits (e.g., Agreeableness, Conscientiousness) in LLMs and analyze their impact on IPD decision-making. Our results show that higher Agreeableness and Conscientiousness improve cooperation but increase susceptibility to exploitation, highlighting both the potential and limitations of personality-based steering for aligning AI agents.

papers.title: Beyond Chains of Thought: Benchmarking Latent-Space Reasoning Abilities in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we quantify the internal reasoning abilities (reasoning leaps) of large language models, and to what extent do they engage in complex latent-space computations without explicit token generation?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a benchmark to quantify latent-space reasoning leaps in LLMs, demonstrating that LLMs can perform internal reasoning and that performance varies across models and reasoning domains.
papers.conclusion: LLMs can perform latent-space reasoning, and larger dense models may have greater potential for internal reasoning, which has implications for safety and the need to monitor opaque internal computations.
papers.key_findings:
GPT-4.5 achieves the highest accuracy (74.7%) on the benchmark, outperforming other models like Grok-2 and Llama 3.1 405B.
Smaller models generally perform worse than larger models, but there are exceptions (e.g., Llama 3.1 70B and 405B perform similarly).
Models with MoE architectures (e.g., Llama 4 Maverick, DeepSeek-V3) underperform compared to dense models of similar total parameter count.
Performance varies across reasoning domains, with social, spatial, and temporal reasoning being more challenging than arithmetic, causal, logical, moral, and linguistic reasoning.
Control experiments suggest that models are not merely exploiting heuristics in the main benchmark, but are actually reasoning internally.
papers.limitation:
Models may exploit heuristics rather than engage in genuine reasoning, which is a limitation of the benchmark.
The benchmark cannot reliably determine when models shift from reasoning to heuristic-based strategies.
future_direction: Investigate the conditions under which LLMs rely on heuristics versus genuine internal reasoning.
Develop methods to better monitor latent-space reasoning to ensure the safe deployment of advanced LLMs.
Study the correlation between model size (and architecture) and latent-space reasoning abilities.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can perform reasoning computations both internally within their latent space and externally by generating explicit token sequences like chains of thought. Significant progress in enhancing reasoning abilities has been made by scaling test-time compute. However, understanding and quantifying model-internal reasoning abilities - the inferential "leaps" models make between individual token predictions - remains crucial. This study introduces a benchmark (n = 4,000 items) designed to quantify model-internal reasoning in different domains. We achieve this by having LLMs indicate the correct solution to reasoning problems not through descriptive text, but by selecting a specific language of their initial response token that is different from English, the benchmark language. This not only requires models to reason beyond their context window, but also to overrise their default tendency to respond in the same language as the prompt, thereby posing an additional cognitive strain. We evaluate a set of 18 LLMs, showing significant performance variations, with GPT-4.5 achieving the highest accuracy (74.7%), outperforming models like Grok-2 (67.2%), and Llama 3.1 405B (65.6%). Control experiments and difficulty scaling analyses suggest that while LLMs engage in internal reasoning, we cannot rule out heuristic exploitations under certain conditions, marking an area for future investigation. Our experiments demonstrate that LLMs can "think" via latent-space computations, revealing model-internal inference strategies that need further understanding, especially regarding safety-related concerns such as covert planning, goal-seeking, or deception emerging without explicit token traces.

papers.title: Exploring the Personality Traits of LLMs through Latent Features Steering
papers.research_question: How do long-term background factors and short-term pressures shape and influence the personality traits of LLMs? How can these factors influence LLMs’ safety?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a training-free method to extract and steer latent features in LLMs to control personality traits, and analyzes the impact of these traits on model safety.
papers.conclusion: The study's method allows for understanding and controlling personality traits in LLMs, which is important for developing personalized AI systems aligned with human values.
papers.key_findings:
Larger models (9B) show more stable personality traits under feature steering compared to smaller models (2B).
Extracted features effectively steer model behavior in social bias tasks, as shown by increased logit differences.
Personality traits can be manipulated by steering long-term background and short-term pressure features.
Safety is affected by personality traits; for example, offensive content is highly sensitive to changes in background features.
The method enables fine-grained control of personality without retraining.
papers.limitation: Training SAEs for LLMs requires substantial computational resources, so the experiments were limited to using pre-trained SAE models, which may limit generalizability to larger-scale models.
future_direction: Explore more efficient methods for extracting precise internal features and enabling fine-grained control of model behavior.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have significantly advanced dialogue systems and role-playing agents through their ability to generate human-like text. While prior studies have shown that LLMs can exhibit distinct and consistent personalities, the mechanisms through which these models encode and express specific personality traits remain poorly understood. To address this, we investigate how various factors, such as cultural norms and environmental stressors, encoded within LLMs, shape their personality traits, guided by the theoretical framework of social determinism. Inspired by related work on LLM interpretability, we propose a training-free approach to modify the model's behavior by extracting and steering latent features corresponding to factors within the model, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of these factors for model safety, focusing on their impact through the lens of personality.

papers.title: Beyond Prompt Engineering: Robust Behavior Control in LLMs via Steering Target Atoms
papers.research_question: How can we achieve precise control over language model generation by isolating and manipulating disentangled knowledge components (target atoms) using sparse autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Steering Target Atoms (STA), a method that uses SAE-decoupled representations to identify and manipulate target atoms for precise behavior control in LLMs, demonstrating improved safety and robustness over prompt engineering and other steering methods.
papers.conclusion: STA provides a novel method for precise behavior control in LLMs, offering superior robustness and flexibility compared to prompt engineering, and can be extended to control reasoning in large reasoning models.
papers.key_findings:
STA achieves state-of-the-art detoxification performance on safety benchmarks, with minimal side effects on general capabilities.
Steering strategies (including STA) are more robust and flexible than prompt engineering, especially in adversarial scenarios.
Steering vectors remain effective even with very few instances (as few as 4).
Steering can control the length of chain-of-thought reasoning in large reasoning models, mitigating overthinking.
Steering in intermediate layers (layers 24-25) is more effective for behavior control.
papers.limitation:
SAE-based methods can be outperformed by simple baselines in some steering tasks, and STA shows limited effectiveness in the personality domain.
Experiments are limited to Gemma and Llama models due to limited public SAE availability.
The study focuses on safety and personality domains; applicability to other domains like multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning is not validated.
future_direction: Extend STA to a broader range of LLMs, including larger and more diverse architectures.
Validate STA in other nuanced domains such as multi-turn dialogue or complex reasoning tasks.
Further investigate the performance divergence of SAE-based methods in different domains.
papers.abstract: Precise control over language model generation is vital for ensuring both safety and reliability. Although prompt engineering and steering are commonly used to intervene in model behaviors, the vast number of parameters in models often results in highly intertwined internal representations. This interdependency can limit control precision and sometimes lead to unintended side effects. Recent research has explored the use of sparse autoencoders (SAE) to disentangle knowledge in high-dimensional spaces for steering. However, these applications have been limited to toy tasks owing to the nontrivial issue of locating atomic knowledge components. In this paper, we propose Steering Target Atoms (STA), a novel method that isolates and manipulates disentangled knowledge components to enhance safety. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Further analysis reveals that steering exhibits superior robustness and flexibility, particularly in adversarial scenarios. We also apply the steering strategy to the large reasoning model, confirming its effectiveness in precise reasoning control.

papers.title: Mind Scramble: Unveiling Large Language Model Psychology Via Typoglycemia
papers.research_question: Does LLM possess human-like cognitive processes and mechanisms in reading and comprehending? The paper uses Typoglycemia to explore this.
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces LLM Psychology, a framework that uses Typoglycemia experiments to study cognitive behaviors of LLMs. It finds that LLMs exhibit human-like behaviors but are fundamentally data-driven, and each LLM has a unique cognitive pattern.
papers.conclusion: The study advances research on aligning LLMs with human cognition and provides evidence that LLMs' abilities are data-driven, offering a case for LLM Psychology.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as slightly lower task accuracy with consuming more tokens and time.
Different LLMs show varying degrees of robustness to scrambled input, making it a democratized benchmark for model evaluation.
The impact of different task types varies, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) in scrambled format being more challenging.
LLMs' emergent human-like abilities are fundamentally statistical and data-driven, rather than genuinely resembling human cognition.
Each LLM exhibits its unique and consistent 'cognitive pattern' across various tasks, unveiling a general mechanism in its psychology process.
papers.abstract: Research into the external behaviors and internal mechanisms of large language models (LLMs) has shown promise in addressing complex tasks in the physical world. Studies suggest that powerful LLMs, like GPT-4, are beginning to exhibit human-like cognitive abilities, including planning, reasoning, and reflection. In this paper, we introduce a research line and methodology called LLM Psychology, leveraging human psychology experiments to investigate the cognitive behaviors and mechanisms of LLMs. We migrate the Typoglycemia phenomenon from psychology to explore the "mind" of LLMs. Unlike human brains, which rely on context and word patterns to comprehend scrambled text, LLMs use distinct encoding and decoding processes. Through Typoglycemia experiments at the character, word, and sentence levels, we observe: (I) LLMs demonstrate human-like behaviors on a macro scale, such as lower task accuracy and higher token/time consumption; (II) LLMs exhibit varying robustness to scrambled input, making Typoglycemia a benchmark for model evaluation without new datasets; (III) Different task types have varying impacts, with complex logical tasks (e.g., math) being more challenging in scrambled form; (IV) Each LLM has a unique and consistent "cognitive pattern" across tasks, revealing general mechanisms in its psychology process. We provide an in-depth analysis of hidden layers to explain these phenomena, paving the way for future research in LLM Psychology and deeper interpretability.

papers.title: When Thinking Backfires: Mechanistic Insights Into Reasoning-Induced Misalignment
papers.abstract: With the growing accessibility and wide adoption of large language models, concerns about their safety and alignment with human values have become paramount. In this paper, we identify a concerning phenomenon: Reasoning-Induced Misalignment (RIM), in which misalignment emerges when reasoning capabilities strengthened-particularly when specific types of reasoning patterns are introduced during inference or training. Beyond reporting this vulnerability, we provide the first mechanistic account of its origins. Through representation analysis, we discover that specific attention heads facilitate refusal by reducing their attention to CoT tokens, a mechanism that modulates the model's rationalization process during inference. During training, we find significantly higher activation entanglement between reasoning and safety in safety-critical neurons than in control neurons, particularly after fine-tuning with those identified reasoning patterns. This entanglement strongly correlates with catastrophic forgetting, providing a neuron-level explanation for RIM.

papers.title: The Reasoning-Memorization Interplay in Language Models Is Mediated by a Single Direction
papers.research_question: What are the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation, and can we identify linear features that mediate this interplay?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies linear reasoning features (LiReFs) in the residual stream of LLMs that mediate the switch between reasoning and memorization, and shows that intervening on these features can improve reasoning performance and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that linear reasoning features in the residual stream mediate the reasoning-memorization interplay in LLMs, and that targeted intervention on these features can enhance reasoning performance and generalizability, offering insights for more robust and interpretable AI systems.
papers.key_findings:
Linear Reasoning Features (LiReFs) can be extracted from the residual stream by contrasting reasoning-intensive and memory-intensive questions.
LiReFs separate questions by their required capability (reasoning vs. memory) across domains and languages.
The activation along LiReFs correlates with the reasoning score assigned by GPT-4o, indicating a spectrum from memory to reasoning.
Inference-time intervention on LiReFs (adding or ablating) can improve model performance on both memory and reasoning tasks.
LiReF intervention enhances genuine reasoning generalizability, as shown on GSM-Symbolic, and reduces reasoning errors.
papers.limitation: The study's definition of memorization as poor generalizability may not capture other forms of memorization (e.g., counterfactual memorization).
future_direction: Investigate whether perturbational and counterfactual memorization are mechanistically equivalent and mediated by LiReFs.
Extend the LiReF analysis to more models and tasks.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel on a variety of reasoning benchmarks, but previous studies suggest they sometimes struggle to generalize to unseen questions, potentially due to over-reliance on memorized training examples. However, the precise conditions under which LLMs switch between reasoning and memorization during text generation remain unclear. In this work, we provide a mechanistic understanding of LLMs' reasoning-memorization dynamics by identifying a set of linear features in the model's residual stream that govern the balance between genuine reasoning and memory recall. These features not only distinguish reasoning tasks from memory-intensive ones but can also be manipulated to causally influence model performance on reasoning tasks. Additionally, we show that intervening in these reasoning features helps the model more accurately activate the most relevant problem-solving capabilities during answer generation. Our findings offer new insights into the underlying mechanisms of reasoning and memory in LLMs and pave the way for the development of more robust and interpretable generative AI systems.

papers.title: Feeling the Strength but Not the Source: Partial Introspection in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can large language models introspect, that is, accurately detect perturbations to their own internal states?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that apparent introspective success in binary detection tasks is explained by global logit shifts, but models exhibit partial introspection on differential tasks (localization and strength comparison) only for early-layer injections, with a mechanistic account based on attention routing and residual stream recovery.
papers.conclusion: The paper finds evidence for partial introspection in LLMs, but only for early-layer injections and on tasks requiring differential sensitivity, cautioning against treating self-reports as reliable safety signals and suggesting introspection relies on general-purpose computational mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Binary detection accuracy is fully explained by intervention-induced global logit shifts that bias models toward affirmative responses, not genuine introspection.
Models can localize which of ten sentences received an injection (up to 88% accuracy) and discriminate relative injection strengths (up to 83% accuracy) far above chance, but only for injections in early layers (L0-L5).
Introspection capabilities are layer-dependent: performance collapses to chance for injections in later layers (L15+).
Mechanistically, attention heads detect perturbations across all layers, but successful introspection requires sufficient downstream computational depth (layers 4-20) for signal integration before residual recovery dynamics attenuate the perturbation.
The residual stream actively recovers from perturbations over subsequent layers, exponentially attenuating the injection signal, explaining why late-layer injections fail to influence outputs.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to a single model (Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct), so generalizability to other models is unknown.
Introspection capabilities are only observed for early-layer injections and not for late layers.
Binary detection tasks are confounded by global logit shifts, which may lead to overestimation of introspection.
future_direction: Evaluate whether these effects scale with model size and architecture (e.g., recurrence/looping that extends the integration window).
Stress-test robustness under adversarial prompts, distribution shift, and multiple simultaneous injections.
Compare native self-report to trained activation-to-language systems and fine-tuned introspection models on bias-resistant localization and strength benchmarks.
papers.abstract: Recent work from Anthropic claims that frontier models can sometimes detect and name injected "concepts" represented as activation directions. We test the robustness of these claims. First, we reproduce Anthropic's multi-turn "emergent introspection" result on Meta-Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, finding that the model identifies and names the injected concept 20 percent of the time under Anthropic's original pipeline, exactly matching their reported numbers and thus showing that introspection is not exclusive to very large or capable models. Second, we systematically vary the inference prompt and find that introspection is fragile: performance collapses on closely related tasks such as multiple-choice identification of the injected concept or different prompts of binary discrimination of whether a concept was injected at all. Third, we identify a contrasting regime of partial introspection: the same model can reliably classify the strength of the coefficient of a normalized injected concept vector (as weak / moderate / strong / very strong) with up to 70 percent accuracy, far above the 25 percent chance baseline. Together, these results provide more evidence for Anthropic's claim that language models effectively compute a function of their baseline, internal representations during introspection; however, these self-reports about those representations are narrow and prompt-sensitive. Our code is available at https://github.com/elyhahami18/CS2881-Introspection.

papers.title: Meaning without reference in large language models
papers.research_question: Can large language models achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, even without direct reference to the real world?
papers.core_contribution: Argues that large language models can achieve meaning through conceptual role theory, where meaning is derived from the relationships between internal representational states, rather than requiring reference to the real world.
papers.conclusion: LLMs likely already share the foundation of how human concepts get their meaning through conceptual role theory.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs likely capture important aspects of meaning through conceptual role, approximating human cognition.
Meaning arises from the interrelations between concepts, which LLMs can learn from text prediction.
Reference is not necessary for meaning; many meaningful concepts lack referents.
LLMs' internal geometries and trajectories approximate those of humans, supporting conceptual role theory.
Text provides clues to conceptual role because human conceptual roles generated the text.
papers.limitation: LLMs do not perfectly capture human concepts and lack aspects like reference, inference, better compositionality, and consistent abstract reasoning.
future_direction: Enrich the internal conceptual roles of LLMs to better reflect human structure, inference, and algorithmic sophistication.
Incorporate multimodal data and experience to improve meaning.
papers.abstract: The widespread success of large language models (LLMs) has been met with skepticism that they possess anything like human concepts or meanings. Contrary to claims that LLMs possess no meaning whatsoever, we argue that they likely capture important aspects of meaning, and moreover work in a way that approximates a compelling account of human cognition in which meaning arises from conceptual role. Because conceptual role is defined by the relationships between internal representational states, meaning cannot be determined from a model's architecture, training data, or objective function, but only by examination of how its internal states relate to each other. This approach may clarify why and how LLMs are so successful and suggest how they can be made more human-like.

papers.title: Measuring Faithfulness in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning faithfully explain the model's actual reasoning process?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes tests for measuring faithfulness of chain-of-thought reasoning and finds that faithfulness varies across tasks and model sizes, with smaller models often producing more faithful reasoning.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful, but it can be faithful under carefully chosen circumstances such as model size and task. Smaller models may be better to use if faithful reasoning is important.
papers.key_findings:
Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer.
CoT's performance boost does not come from added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT.
As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks studied.
Smaller models often generate more faithful reasoning than larger, more capable ones.
Faithfulness depends on model size and task difficulty, with easier tasks and larger models leading to less faithful reasoning.
papers.limitation:
Lack of ground truth about the model's internal reasoning process, making it impossible to know if CoT is truly faithful.
Analysis limited to RLHF-finetuned models; faithfulness may differ for pretrained LLMs or other training schemes.
future_direction: Investigate training schemes different from RLHF for eliciting more faithful reasoning.
Use the proposed metrics to increase the faithfulness of CoT and build systems with trustworthy reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform better when they produce step-by-step, "Chain-of-Thought" (CoT) reasoning before answering a question, but it is unclear if the stated reasoning is a faithful explanation of the model's actual reasoning (i.e., its process for answering the question). We investigate hypotheses for how CoT reasoning may be unfaithful, by examining how the model predictions change when we intervene on the CoT (e.g., by adding mistakes or paraphrasing it). Models show large variation across tasks in how strongly they condition on the CoT when predicting their answer, sometimes relying heavily on the CoT and other times primarily ignoring it. CoT's performance boost does not seem to come from CoT's added test-time compute alone or from information encoded via the particular phrasing of the CoT. As models become larger and more capable, they produce less faithful reasoning on most tasks we study. Overall, our results suggest that CoT can be faithful if the circumstances such as the model size and task are carefully chosen.

papers.title: Mechanistic Evidence for Faithfulness Decay in Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: Does chain-of-thought reasoning reflect the model's actual decision-making process, or is it merely post-hoc justification?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces NLDD, a metric for step-level faithfulness in chain-of-thought reasoning, and discovers a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70–85% of chain length beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer.
papers.conclusion: NLDD quantifies the causal influence of reasoning chains on model predictions, revealing that high accuracy can mask a lack of causal dependence on CoT, and identifies a reasoning horizon beyond which steps contribute minimally or negatively.
papers.key_findings:
Different architectures exhibit distinct faithfulness patterns (faithful vs. anti-faithful regimes).
The Mapping Gap demonstrates models can encode task-relevant structure in internal representations without utilizing it for prediction.
The reasoning horizon (k*) is a consistent transition point at 70-85% of chain length where causal influence decays.
NLDD reveals failure modes that accuracy-based evaluation misses, such as anti-faithful behavior.
For anti-faithful models, extended reasoning beyond the horizon can be harmful, acting as a causal distractor.
papers.limitation:
Truncates chains rather than replacing corrupted steps, which conflates weak reliance on a step with sufficiency of prior steps.
Logit normalization assumes architectural differences affect margins and variance proportionally, which is empirically supported but not guaranteed.
TAS and RSA analysis uses a single middle layer; layer-wise variation is small but comprehensive analysis may reveal depth-dependent effects.
Evaluation is limited to three tasks (100 samples each), two of which are synthetic, and to decoder-only models.
Uses greedy decoding with fixed prompts; stochastic decoding may shift horizon locations.
Step-based analysis assumes explicit chain structure; free-form CoT would require different segmentation.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) explanations are widely used to interpret how language models solve complex problems, yet it remains unclear whether these step-by-step explanations reflect how the model actually reaches its answer, or merely post-hoc justifications. We propose Normalized Logit Difference Decay (NLDD), a metric that measures whether individual reasoning steps are faithful to the model's decision-making process. Our approach corrupts individual reasoning steps from the explanation and measures how much the model's confidence in its answer drops, to determine if a step is truly important. By standardizing these measurements, NLDD enables rigorous cross-model comparison across different architectures. Testing three model families across syntactic, logical, and arithmetic tasks, we discover a consistent Reasoning Horizon (k*) at 70--85% of chain length, beyond which reasoning tokens have little or negative effect on the final answer. We also find that models can encode correct internal representations while completely failing the task. These results show that accuracy alone does not reveal whether a model actually reasons through its chain. NLDD offers a way to measure when CoT matters.

papers.title: ShortGPT: Layers in Large Language Models are More Redundant Than You Expect
papers.research_question: How redundant are the layers in large language models, and can a simple layer removal method based on a new importance metric effectively prune them?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies significant layer redundancy in LLMs and introduces Block Influence (BI) to measure layer importance. Based on BI, the proposed ShortGPT method removes redundant layers, achieving competitive pruning results without fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: LLMs exhibit significant layer-wise redundancy, and a simple pruning method based on layer removal (ShortGPT) can effectively compress models with minimal performance loss, offering insights for future model compression and training efficiency.
papers.key_findings:
Layers in LLMs are redundant, especially in the middle to later layers, and removing them individually causes minimal performance degradation.
The proposed Block Influence (BI) metric, based on cosine similarity between a layer's input and output hidden states, correlates with layer importance.
ShortGPT, a simple layer removal method based on BI, outperforms previous state-of-the-art pruning methods and maintains ~90% performance while reducing ~25% parameters.
The redundancy phenomenon is not unique to transformers; it also exists in non-transformer models like Mamba and RWKV.
ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization and can be combined with it for further compression.
papers.limitation: Layer removal has a more significant negative effect on generative tasks compared to multiple-choice tasks, especially for smaller models.
future_direction: Exploring post-training to restore performance after pruning
Improving model training efficiency by reducing inherent redundancy
papers.abstract: As Large Language Models (LLMs) continue to advance in performance, their size has escalated significantly, with current LLMs containing billions or even trillions of parameters. However, in this study, we discovered that many layers of LLMs exhibit high similarity, and some layers play a negligible role in network functionality. Based on this observation, we define a metric called Block Influence (BI) to gauge the significance of each layer in LLMs. We then propose a straightforward pruning approach: layer removal, in which we directly delete the redundant layers in LLMs based on their BI scores. Experiments demonstrate that our method, which we call ShortGPT, significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in model pruning. Moreover, ShortGPT is orthogonal to quantization-like methods, enabling further reduction in parameters and computation. The ability to achieve better results through simple layer removal, as opposed to more complex pruning techniques, suggests a high degree of redundancy in the model architecture.

papers.title: Beyond Words: A Latent Memory Approach to Internal Reasoning in LLMs
papers.research_question: Can incorporating implicit mental representations (latent memory) into LLMs lead to more efficient internal reasoning compared to explicit chain-of-thought reasoning?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework that integrates an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into LLMs to enhance internal reasoning efficiency using latent representations, demonstrating reduced training loss compared to a baseline model.
papers.conclusion: The Implicit Memory Module framework improves model efficiency for internal reasoning, and future work can explore integrating explicit interpretability channels without compromising computational gains.
papers.key_findings:
Incorporating the IMM into a GPT model reduced final training loss by 35% to 57% across different context window sizes.
The IMM is designed to be computationally efficient and scalable, with overhead that is minimal compared to standard transformer operations.
The framework allows for optional integration of an explicit chain-of-thought decoder for interpretability without burdening the core inference process.
Preliminary experiments on adaptive long-term memory during inference revealed challenges including increased computational cost, stability issues, and security risks.
papers.limitation:
Preliminary experiments were conducted on a small dataset (Shakespeare) with limited context windows.
Attempts at adaptive long-term memory during inference increased computational costs, introduced stability issues like catastrophic forgetting, and posed potential security risks.
future_direction: Explore safer and more effective methods to incorporate explicit auditability without compromising computational efficiency, such as lightweight chain-of-thought decoders.
Conduct further theoretical analysis and ablation studies, such as varying the number of memory slots and testing different summarization strategies.
papers.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have popularized the chain-of-thought (CoT) paradigm, in which models produce explicit reasoning steps in natural language. Although this approach improves interpretability and facilitates external auditing, it may not represent the most computationally efficient method for internal reasoning. In contrast, human cognition relies on implicit mental representations that recall past sensory and episodic information without requiring complete verbalization. In this paper, we propose a framework that integrates implicit mental representations into the internal reasoning processes of LLMs. Preliminary experiments indicate that incorporating an Implicit Memory Module (IMM) into a simple GPT model yields a reduction of between 35% and 57% in final training loss compared to a regular GPT baseline. The addition of an explicit interpretability channel (e.g., a chain-of-thought decoder) is straightforward to implement within this approach. We outline theoretical foundations, propose technical mechanisms to scale the memory module, and discuss how these ideas may lead to more efficient and robust reasoning, with optional future extensions for explicit auditability.

papers.title: Analyzing Machine‐Learned Representations: A Natural Language Case Study
papers.research_question: To what extent do machine-learned sentence embeddings encode and utilize abstract, composable relational structure for natural language inference, and how does the training distribution influence the learned representations and heuristics?
papers.core_contribution: This paper uses cognitive science methods to analyze sentence embeddings, revealing that a state-of-the-art model (InferSent) relies on simple, ecologically valid heuristics (overlap, antonyms, negation) rather than abstract compositional rules for NLI, but can learn such rules with targeted training data augmentation, albeit with limitations in generalization (context-tying).
papers.conclusion: Methods from cognitive science and psycholinguistics, such as diagnostic test sets, provide valuable insights into machine-learned representations, revealing heuristic strategies and their origins in training data. While augmentation can encourage learning of abstract rules, limitations like context-tying suggest tabula rasa neural networks may require combinatorially large data or built-in inductive biases to achieve human-like systematicity.
papers.key_findings:
InferSent sentence embeddings perform poorly on a diagnostic test set (Comparisons dataset) requiring abstract relational reasoning, achieving near-chance accuracy.
Analysis of InferSent's errors reveals it uses heuristic strategies (overlap, antonyms, negation) that are ecologically valid in the SNLI training data.
When fine-tuned or trained on an augmented dataset containing examples of the abstract rules, InferSent can achieve near-perfect performance on the diagnostic test and generalize to unseen words (zero-shot reasoning).
However, the learned representations exhibit 'context-tying': generalization is poor for words previously seen only in a different syntactic context, analogous to human belief bias.
The training distribution has a strong effect on the representations learned, and simple heuristics can be learned instead of systematic rules if they explain variance in the training data.
papers.limitation:
The learned representations exhibit 'context-tying', hindering generalization of abstract rules to words seen previously in different contexts.
Achieving fully systematic representations via data augmentation alone may require combinatorially large amounts of training data.
future_direction: Study how systematicity evolves over the course of augmented training and how much augmentation is needed.
Integrate top-down knowledge of language structure with methods that learn to generate adversarial augmentations.
Build useful inductive biases into models to scalably learn systematic representations.
Use diagnostic metrics like context-tying to benchmark systematicity in other domains (e.g., scene understanding, planning).
papers.abstract: As modern deep networks become more complex, and get closer to human-like capabilities in certain domains, the question arises as to how the representations and decision rules they learn compare to the ones in humans. In this work, we study representations of sentences in one such artificial system for natural language processing. We first present a diagnostic test dataset to examine the degree of abstract composable structure represented. Analyzing performance on these diagnostic tests indicates a lack of systematicity in representations and decision rules, and reveals a set of heuristic strategies. We then investigate the effect of training distribution on learning these heuristic strategies, and we study changes in these representations with various augmentations to the training set. Our results reveal parallels to the analogous representations in people. We find that these systems can learn abstract rules and generalize them to new contexts under certain circumstances-similar to human zero-shot reasoning. However, we also note some shortcomings in this generalization behavior-similar to human judgment errors like belief bias. Studying these parallels suggests new ways to understand psychological phenomena in humans as well as informs best strategies for building artificial intelligence with human-like language understanding.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: Only a core nucleus of attention heads and feed forward networks (FFNs) in a large language model (OPT-66B) are important for in-context learning across a wide variety of tasks, and these important heads overlap with task-agnostic induction heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, and the findings motivate investigating pre-training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
~70% of attention heads and ~20% of FFNs can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in the intermediate layers of the model.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples (shots).
A small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on primitive induction operations (prefix matching and copying).
These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, indicating they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
papers.limitation:
No causal link is claimed between induction heads and sophisticated in-context learning capabilities; deeper investigation is needed.
The study uses only up to 5 in-context examples and random selection of examples.
All downstream tasks are monolingual.
future_direction: Increase the number and strength of induction heads via auxiliary pre-training objectives for primitives like prefix matching and copying.
Investigate and improve (pre-)training regimes to increase the number of important model components for in-context learning.
Replicate the study with instruction-tuned model variants (e.g., OPT-IML).
papers.abstract: Hritik Bansal, Karthik Gopalakrishnan, Saket Dingliwal, Sravan Bodapati, Katrin Kirchhoff, Dan Roth. Proceedings of the 61st Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (Volume 1: Long Papers). 2023.

papers.title: Why Can GPT Learn In-Context? Language Models Implicitly Perform Gradient Descent as Meta-Optimizers
papers.research_question: What is the working mechanism of in-context learning (ICL) in GPT models? The paper investigates whether ICL can be understood as implicit finetuning, where the attention mechanism performs a form of gradient descent.
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent, leading to the understanding that in-context learning is a form of implicit finetuning. Inspired by this, the paper designs a momentum-based attention mechanism that improves performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that in-context learning can be understood as implicit finetuning via a meta-optimization process, and this understanding can inspire model design, as demonstrated by the momentum-based attention.
papers.key_findings:
Transformer attention has a dual form with gradient descent, which explains in-context learning as implicit finetuning.
Empirical comparisons show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning in terms of predictions, attention outputs, attention weights, and attention to training tokens.
Momentum-based attention, designed by analogy with gradient descent with momentum, improves performance on language modeling and in-context learning tasks.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is limited to Transformer-based models and does not consider other architectures.
The dual form is derived using a relaxed linear attention approximation, and the mechanism of standard attention without approximation may be more complex.
Experiments are limited to models up to 2.7B parameters and only classification tasks, leaving larger models and other task types for future work.
future_direction: Study in-context learning for non-Transformer architectures.
Investigate the mechanism of standard Transformer attention without the linear approximation.
Extend the analysis to larger models and other tasks like open-ended generation.
papers.abstract: Large pretrained language models have shown surprising in-context learning (ICL) ability. With a few demonstration input-label pairs, they can predict the label for an unseen input without parameter updates. Despite the great success in performance, its working mechanism still remains an open question. In this paper, we explain language models as meta-optimizers and understand in-context learning as implicit finetuning. Theoretically, we figure out that Transformer attention has a dual form of gradient descent. On top of it, we understand ICL as follows: GPT first produces meta-gradients according to the demonstration examples, and then these meta-gradients are applied to the original GPT to build an ICL model. We comprehensively compare the behaviors of in-context learning and explicit finetuning on real tasks to provide empirical evidence that supports our understanding. Experimental results show that in-context learning behaves similarly to explicit finetuning from multiple perspectives. Inspired by the dual form between Transformer attention and gradient descent, we design a momentum-based attention by analogy with gradient descent with momentum. The improved performance over vanilla attention further supports our understanding from another perspective, and more importantly, shows the potential to utilize our understanding for future model design. The code is available at \url{https://aka.ms/icl}.

papers.title: Can LLMs Lie? Investigation beyond Hallucination
papers.research_question: This paper investigates whether LLMs can intentionally lie (as opposed to unintentionally hallucinate), and how to understand and control lying behavior using mechanistic interpretability.
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers the neural mechanisms of lying in LLMs using mechanistic interpretability, and introduces steering vectors to control lying behavior, showing a trade-off between honesty and task performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that lying in LLMs can be understood and controlled via mechanistic interpretability, and highlights the trade-offs between honesty and task success in real-world scenarios.
papers.key_findings:
Lying ability in LLMs improves with model size and reasoning capabilities.
LLMs use dummy tokens as a computational scratchpad for lying, with specific attention heads and MLP modules involved.
Lying circuits are sparse and can be ablated to reduce deception without broadly degrading model utility.
Different types of lies (white vs. malicious, commission vs. omission) are linearly separable in activation space and controllable via distinct steering directions.
Steering vectors can increase honesty in multi-turn conversational settings, establishing a Pareto frontier between honesty and goal completion.
papers.limitation:
Analysis confined to a few model families and sizes.
Steering vectors derived from a limited set of contrastive prompts.
Multi-turn conversational setting is simplified.
Honesty steering vectors applied in the negative direction may lead to mass production of false information.
future_direction: Scaling the approach to larger models and more complex scenarios.
Investigating the transferability of steering vectors across domains.
Developing more robust safeguards against deceptive AI.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities across a variety of tasks, but their increasing autonomy in real-world applications raises concerns about their trustworthiness. While hallucinations-unintentional falsehoods-have been widely studied, the phenomenon of lying, where an LLM knowingly generates falsehoods to achieve an ulterior objective, remains underexplored. In this work, we systematically investigate the lying behavior of LLMs, differentiating it from hallucinations and testing it in practical scenarios. Through mechanistic interpretability techniques, we uncover the neural mechanisms underlying deception, employing logit lens analysis, causal interventions, and contrastive activation steering to identify and control deceptive behavior. We study real-world lying scenarios and introduce behavioral steering vectors that enable fine-grained manipulation of lying tendencies. Further, we explore the trade-offs between lying and end-task performance, establishing a Pareto frontier where dishonesty can enhance goal optimization. Our findings contribute to the broader discourse on AI ethics, shedding light on the risks and potential safeguards for deploying LLMs in high-stakes environments. Code and more illustrations are available at https://llm-liar.github.io/

papers.title: Unveiling Transformers with LEGO: a synthetic reasoning task
papers.research_question: How do Transformer architectures learn to follow a chain of reasoning, and how do architectural choices (like weight tying) and data composition (like pretraining) affect their generalization and the emergence of specific attention patterns?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the LEGO synthetic reasoning task to study how Transformers learn to follow chains of reasoning. It identifies that successful models develop specialized attention heads for association (long-range identity matching) and manipulation (short-range operations), and based on this insight, proposes the LEGO attention module which reduces FLOPs while maintaining or improving performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.conclusion: The LEGO task provides a controlled setting to understand how Transformers learn reasoning, revealing the importance of structured attention patterns for generalization. These insights can guide architectural design, as demonstrated by the proposed LEGO attention module which offers efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
Classical generalization can be deceptive, as models can learn 'shortcut' solutions that do not follow the intended chain of reasoning and impede out-of-distribution generalization.
Iterative architectures like ALBERT, which share weights across layers, exhibit better length extrapolation (generalization to longer reasoning chains) than non-iterative architectures like BERT, suggesting an inductive bias towards implementing a 'for-loop'.
Pretraining helps generalization on the LEGO task primarily by providing a beneficial initialization with structured attention patterns (association and manipulation heads), rather than by encoding complex task-specific knowledge.
Models can be incentivized to learn more robust, iterative solutions through techniques like stochastic depth training, which improves length extrapolation.
The identified structured attention patterns motivate a new LEGO attention module, which when used as a drop-in replacement for standard attention, reduces computational cost and matches or improves performance in large-scale pretraining.
papers.limitation: The study uses a synthetic task, which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world reasoning tasks.
future_direction: Applying the insights from the LEGO task to currently challenging mathematical reasoning tasks like MATH and IsarStep.
Exploring the application of the LEGO attention module to other domains and tasks.
papers.abstract: We propose a synthetic reasoning task, LEGO (Learning Equality and Group Operations), that encapsulates the problem of following a chain of reasoning, and we study how the Transformer architectures learn this task. We pay special attention to data effects such as pretraining (on seemingly unrelated NLP tasks) and dataset composition (e.g., differing chain length at training and test time), as well as architectural variants such as weight-tied layers or adding convolutional components. We study how the trained models eventually succeed at the task, and in particular, we manage to understand some of the attention heads as well as how the information flows in the network. In particular, we have identified a novel \emph{association} pattern that globally attends only to identical tokens. Based on these observations we propose a hypothesis that here pretraining helps for LEGO tasks due to certain structured attention patterns, and we experimentally verify this hypothesis. We also observe that in some data regime the trained transformer finds ``shortcut" solutions to follow the chain of reasoning, which impedes the model's robustness, and moreover we propose ways to prevent it. Motivated by our findings on structured attention patterns, we propose the LEGO attention module, a drop-in replacement for vanilla attention heads. This architectural change significantly reduces Flops and maintains or even \emph{improves} the model's performance at large-scale pretraining.

papers.title: The Geometry of Harmfulness in LLMs through Subconcept Probing
papers.research_question: How can we understand and mitigate harmful behaviors in LLMs by decomposing harmfulness into subconcepts and analyzing their geometric structure in activation space?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that harmfulness in LLMs can be represented as a low-rank linear subspace in activation space, and steering in the dominant direction of this subspace can effectively reduce harmful generations with minimal utility loss.
papers.conclusion: The work presents a geometric approach to understanding and mitigating harmfulness in LLMs, underscoring the value of multidimensional probing for uncovering latent harmful behaviors and designing more controllable and transparent models.
papers.key_findings:
